title: Congenital Urinary Disease: Alport Syndrome, Cystic Kidneys, Renal Agenesis, and Vesicoureteral Reflux
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers kidney and urinary tract disease that begins with a gene defect or a developmental error: Alport syndrome, the cystic kidney diseases, renal agenesis, and vesicoureteral reflux. Each condition is explained from the molecule or embryologic step that fails to the lesion it produces and the findings it causes outside the kidney, such as deafness, liver disease, brain aneurysms, or Potter sequence. Board items usually give an age, an inheritance pattern, and one extrarenal clue and expect you to name the disorder and explain why that clue belongs to it.

sections.title: Alport syndrome: a defective type IV collagen network

blocks.text: Alport syndrome is a hereditary disease of type IV collagen that damages the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), the cochlea, and the eye. Type IV collagen forms sheets rather than fibrils: three alpha chains wind into a triple helix (a protomer), and protomers join end to end and side by side into a network that gives the basement membrane its strength.
Why one chain defect breaks the whole network

The embryonic GBM uses an alpha 1, alpha 1, alpha 2 network. During glomerular maturation, podocytes switch to producing alpha 3, alpha 4, and alpha 5 chains, which assemble together into one protomer. This mature network has more cross-links and resists proteolysis better, so it lasts under the high filtration pressure of the glomerulus. Because each protomer needs all three chains, loss of any one prevents the mature network from forming. The embryonic network persists in its place, and over years it thins, frays, and splits.

blocks.title: Genetics of Alport syndrome
rows: Hemizygous males; carrier females vary from isolated hematuria to renal failure
Males and females equally, with severe early disease
Milder, later disease in both sexes
blocks.caption: Every form causes the same failure: the alpha 3, 4, 5 protomer cannot assemble. Proportions are approximate and vary by source.

blocks.text: Males with the X-linked form have no normal alpha 5 chain, so the mature network is absent in every glomerulus. Carrier females are mosaics: random X inactivation leaves some podocytes making normal alpha 5 and others not, so disease ranges from microscopic hematuria alone to renal failure later in life.

blocks.text: Clinical course and extrarenal findings

Persistent microscopic hematuria is present from early childhood, with episodes of gross hematuria in some children, often after a respiratory infection. The hematuria is glomerular, so red cells are dysmorphic and red cell casts may appear. Proteinuria, hypertension, and declining GFR follow, and most males with X-linked disease reach end-stage renal disease by about 20 to 40 years of age. The same alpha 3, 4, 5 network lines the basement membranes of the cochlea and the lens capsule. Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, beginning in high frequencies, develops in later childhood and is not present at birth. A thin anterior lens capsule lets the lens bulge forward as anterior lenticonus; dot and fleck retinopathy is also seen.

Light microscopy is nonspecific early and later shows glomerulosclerosis, interstitial fibrosis, and lipid-laden interstitial foam cells. Electron microscopy is diagnostic: the lamina densa is thin in some segments and thickened and split into interweaving layers in others, the basket-weave pattern. Immunostaining shows absent alpha 5 chain in the GBM, and in X-linked males also in the epidermal basement membrane of skin. Thin basement membrane disease, often from one abnormal COL4A3 or COL4A4 allele, causes uniform GBM thinning with benign familial hematuria and no deafness. Anti-GBM disease is the immune mirror image: its antibodies target the alpha 3 chain, and a few Alport patients form anti-GBM antibodies after transplantation because the normal alpha 3, 4, 5 network of the donor kidney is foreign to an immune system that never encountered it.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common inherited kidney disease, affecting about 1 in 400 to 1 in 1,000 people, and a leading genetic cause of end-stage renal disease. About 85% of cases come from mutations in PKD1 on chromosome 16, which encodes polycystin-1, and most of the rest from PKD2 on chromosome 4, which encodes polycystin-2. PKD2 disease is milder, and renal failure arrives about two decades later.
How a ciliary defect makes a cyst

Polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 form a complex on the primary cilium of tubular cells. When urine flow bends the cilium, polycystin-2 lets calcium enter, which holds cyclic AMP (cAMP) low and keeps the cell quiet and the tubule at a fixed diameter. Without this signal, intracellular calcium falls and cAMP rises. In polycystin-deficient cells, cAMP stimulates proliferation and drives chloride secretion through the CFTR channel, with water following. A tubule segment therefore widens, pinches off from its nephron, and keeps filling by secretion. Vasopressin raises cAMP in collecting duct cells, and blocking its V2 receptor slows cyst growth, which supports this mechanism.

Every cell carries one mutant allele, yet only a small fraction of nephrons become cysts. The usual explanation is a second, somatic hit that inactivates the normal allele in a single tubular cell, which then expands clonally. Cysts therefore appear focally and accumulate over decades, so kidneys are usually normal in childhood and can reach about 4 kg each by late adulthood.

blocks.text: Intracranial aneurysms occur in roughly 10% of patients, clustering in families with a history of aneurysm, and a ruptured aneurysm presents as a sudden severe headache from subarachnoid hemorrhage. Liver cysts rarely impair liver function because hepatocytes are spared. Cardiovascular disease driven by hypertension is a major cause of death. Ultrasound shows enlarged kidneys with multiple bilateral cysts; the number required for diagnosis rises with age because cysts accumulate.

blocks.predict: Why does a patient with ADPKD carry the mutation in every cell from conception yet have normal kidneys at age 10 and huge kidneys at 50?
blocks.explain: A cyst forms only after a second somatic hit inactivates the normal allele in one tubular cell. These hits accumulate randomly over time, and each cyst then grows slowly by proliferation and fluid secretion, so cyst number and size rise with age.

sections.title: ARPKD, multicystic dysplastic kidney, and acquired cystic disease

blocks.text: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease

Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) results from mutations in both alleles of PKHD1 on chromosome 6, which encodes fibrocystin, a ciliary protein of collecting duct and bile duct epithelium. It is uncommon, about 1 in 20,000 births. The collecting ducts dilate into elongated cysts that run at right angles to the capsule, so the cut surface looks spongy with radial channels. Both kidneys are greatly enlarged but keep a smooth surface and their normal shape, unlike the lumpy kidneys of ADPKD.

Severe disease presents before or at birth. Little urine is made in utero, so oligohydramnios produces Potter sequence, and pulmonary hypoplasia is the usual cause of death in the newborn period. In the liver, the embryonic ductal plate fails to remodel, leaving excess, abnormal bile ducts in fibrotic portal tracts. This congenital hepatic fibrosis blocks portal flow before the sinusoids, so children who survive infancy develop portal hypertension with splenomegaly and varices while hepatocyte function stays normal. Children with milder renal disease present later with hypertension and chronic kidney disease, and the liver may dominate.
Multicystic dysplastic kidney

Multicystic dysplastic kidney is a developmental error, not a single-gene disease, and is usually sporadic. The ureteric bud is often atretic or obstructed, so the metanephric mesenchyme is poorly induced and differentiates abnormally. The result is a nonfunctioning mass of cysts. The diagnostic histology is renal dysplasia: primitive ducts lined by immature epithelium, surrounded by undifferentiated mesenchyme, often with islands of cartilage. It is usually unilateral, and the opposite kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy, although that kidney has extra risk of reflux or obstruction. Bilateral disease behaves like bilateral agenesis and is lethal.
Acquired cystic kidney disease

Patients with end-stage kidneys, especially after years of dialysis, develop many cortical and medullary cysts. Cyst number rises with time in renal failure rather than with the dialysis method, which points to uremia and growth stimulation of surviving tubular cells, although the exact signal is not established. The kidneys are usually small or normal in size. Cysts may bleed and cause hematuria, and their lining can transform, so renal cell carcinoma is markedly more common than in the general population.

blocks.title: Three patients with cystic kidneys
blocks.text: A newborn with bilateral smooth, enlarged kidneys was born after oligohydramnios and needs ventilation; years later a sibling has splenomegaly and varices with normal liver enzymes. Bilateral disease at birth, a recessive pattern in siblings, and presinusoidal portal hypertension point to ARPKD with congenital hepatic fibrosis. A second newborn has one nonfunctioning cystic flank mass and a normal opposite kidney; one-sided disease with a working partner points to multicystic dysplastic kidney, and the infant survives because the other kidney makes urine. A 58-year-old man on dialysis for 9 years develops hematuria, and imaging shows many cysts and a solid mass in small kidneys: acquired cystic disease with renal cell carcinoma.

sections.title: Renal agenesis, oligohydramnios, and Potter sequence

blocks.text: The permanent kidney (metanephros) appears in the fifth week, when the ureteric bud grows from the mesonephric duct into the metanephric mesenchyme. The two tissues induce each other. Mesenchymal cells secrete glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), which acts on the RET receptor of the bud and makes it branch into the ureter, pelvis, calyces, and collecting ducts. The bud tips in turn induce the mesenchyme to form nephrons, from Bowman capsule to the distal convoluted tubule. Renal agenesis follows when the bud fails to form, fails to reach the mesenchyme, or fails to induce it.
Why bilateral agenesis is lethal

Fetal urine production begins late in the first trimester, and from about 16 weeks it supplies most of the amniotic fluid. With no kidneys, almost no fluid accumulates. Oligohydramnios has two effects. The uterine wall presses directly on the fetus, deforming the face and limbs and restricting chest expansion. The lungs also fail to grow, because normal lung development needs fluid retained within the airways and fetal breathing movements against a fluid-filled space. The deformities are therefore a sequence, a cascade from one primary defect, rather than separate malformations.

blocks.title: Potter sequence from bilateral renal agenesis

blocks.caption: Pulmonary hypoplasia, not the absent kidneys, causes death in the first hours or days.

blocks.title: Features of Potter sequence

blocks.text: Unilateral agenesis and the single kidney

Unilateral agenesis is far more common, about 1 in 1,000 births, and usually silent because one kidney makes enough urine to keep amniotic fluid normal. The remaining kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy. Nephron number is fixed once nephrogenesis ends at about 34 to 36 weeks of gestation, so the kidney grows by enlarging its existing nephrons: each glomerulus filters more (higher single-nephron GFR), and tubular cells hypertrophy to reabsorb the larger filtered load. Total GFR approaches but usually does not reach that of two kidneys. The same adaptation follows loss of a kidney later in life. Sustained glomerular hyperfiltration can, in some patients over years, cause proteinuria, secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, and hypertension.

Because the ureteric bud arises from the mesonephric duct, which lies beside the paramesonephric duct, unilateral agenesis is often accompanied by genital anomalies on the same side. Males may lack the vas deferens or seminal vesicle on that side, and females may have a unicornuate uterus or a duplicated uterus with an obstructed hemivagina. Renal hypoplasia differs from agenesis: a small kidney with fewer nephrons but normal structure, which also limits nephron mass.

blocks.predict: A fetus has one normal kidney and a contralateral multicystic dysplastic kidney. Will Potter sequence develop?
blocks.explain: No. Amniotic fluid depends on total fetal urine output, and one functioning kidney makes enough, so fluid volume stays normal and the lungs grow. Potter sequence requires failure of both kidneys or blocked outflow from both.

blocks.text: Normally urine moves only downward because the ureterovesical junction works as a flap valve. The distal ureter passes obliquely through the bladder wall and then runs a submucosal tunnel before opening at the trigone. As bladder pressure rises during filling and voiding, that pressure flattens the intravesical segment against the detrusor and seals it. The longer the tunnel relative to the diameter of the ureter, the better the seal.
Primary and secondary reflux

In primary vesicoureteral reflux (VUR), the intravesical segment is congenitally short and the ureteral orifice lies lateral to its usual position, so voiding pressure pushes urine up the ureter instead of closing it. The defect is developmental: a ureteric bud that arises too low on the mesonephric duct is absorbed into the bladder early and ends up with a short tunnel. Primary VUR is found in about 1% of children and in roughly one third of children evaluated after a febrile urinary tract infection, and it is often familial. Secondary VUR occurs when a normal junction is overwhelmed by high bladder pressure, as with posterior urethral valves in boys or a neurogenic bladder.

blocks.title: From short intravesical ureter to reflux nephropathy

Voiding pressure drives urine up the ureter
Refluxed urine returns afterward, leaving residual urine
Bladder bacteria are carried to the renal pelvis
Intrarenal reflux through compound papillae at the poles
Recurrent pyelonephritis with parenchymal inflammation
Polar scars over blunted calyces: reflux nephropathy
Hypertension, proteinuria, chronic kidney disease
blocks.caption: Infection carried into the parenchyma is the main driver of scarring; high-pressure sterile reflux contributes mainly in secondary VUR.

blocks.text: Reflux does two harmful things. Urine that rises into the ureter drains back into the bladder after voiding, so the bladder never fully empties, and residual urine lets bacteria multiply. The same flow also carries those bacteria to the renal pelvis, which is why VUR presents as recurrent febrile urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis in young children. Whether infection reaches the parenchyma depends on papillary shape. Simple papillae, which are convex with slit-like duct openings, close under pressure. Compound papillae, which are flat or concave with gaping ducts and cluster at the upper and lower poles, let urine pass into the collecting ducts (intrarenal reflux).

Inflammation in these regions heals as broad, coarse cortical scars that sit over dilated, blunted calyces, mostly at the poles. This is reflux nephropathy, the classic form of chronic pyelonephritis. As functioning nephrons are lost, the rest hyperfilter, and renin release from scarred regions raises blood pressure, so children and young adults develop hypertension, proteinuria, and chronic kidney disease. Mild primary reflux often resolves with growth because the intravesical tunnel lengthens.
Diagnosis and grading

The voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) is the diagnostic study. Contrast is instilled into the bladder through a catheter, and films are taken during filling and voiding, when bladder pressure peaks and reflux is most likely to appear. It shows whether contrast rises into the ureter and pelvis, grades the reflux, and outlines the urethra, which identifies secondary causes such as posterior urethral valves. Renal ultrasound shows dilation but cannot exclude reflux, and a DMSA nuclear scan shows scars rather than reflux itself.

blocks.title: International grading of reflux on VCUG
rows: Contrast enters the ureter only, without dilation
Reaches pelvis and calyces without dilation
Mild to moderate dilation of ureter and pelvis, mild blunting of calyces
Moderate dilation and tortuosity; calyceal angles lost, papillary impressions kept
Gross dilation and tortuosity; papillary impressions lost
blocks.caption: Higher grade predicts more scarring and less spontaneous resolution.

integration.text: Every disorder in this chapter starts at a defined point in development or in a protein, and the extrarenal findings come from the same point. Type IV collagen alpha 3, 4, and 5 chains shared by the GBM, cochlea, and lens explain the triad of Alport syndrome. Ciliary proteins shared by renal tubules, bile ducts, and arteries explain why ADPKD brings liver cysts and aneurysms, and why ARPKD brings congenital hepatic fibrosis. The ureteric bud, which grows from the mesonephric duct, links renal agenesis to ipsilateral genital anomalies and links primary reflux to an orifice placed too far laterally. Amniotic fluid physiology connects any failure of fetal urine output to the lungs, so bilateral agenesis, severe ARPKD, bilateral dysplasia, and urethral obstruction all produce the same Potter sequence.

The chapter also shows that the kidney responds to lost nephron mass in one way, whatever the cause. A single kidney after agenesis, a kidney opposite a dysplastic one, and the surviving nephrons in reflux nephropathy all hyperfilter, and in some patients this adaptation leads over years to proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis, and hypertension. The limits of these associations matter: carrier females in X-linked Alport syndrome may have only hematuria, many patients with ADPKD never develop an aneurysm, and most children with mild reflux never scar.

summary: Alport syndrome is failure of the alpha 3, 4, 5 type IV collagen network, most often from X-linked COL4A5 mutation, so males are affected most severely.
Alport syndrome causes hematuria progressing to renal failure, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus, with a split, basket-weave GBM on electron microscopy.
ADPKD comes from PKD1 or PKD2 mutation; loss of ciliary polycystin signaling lowers intracellular calcium and raises cAMP, which drives cyst proliferation and fluid secretion.

ADPKD causes bilaterally enlarged cystic kidneys in adults, with flank pain, hematuria, early hypertension, and progressive renal failure; liver cysts are the most common extrarenal finding, and berry aneurysms and mitral valve prolapse also occur.

ARPKD (PKHD1, fibrocystin) presents in infancy with bilaterally enlarged smooth kidneys of radial collecting duct cysts, Potter sequence when severe, and congenital hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension.
Multicystic dysplastic kidney is a sporadic developmental lesion, usually unilateral, with immature ducts, mesenchyme, and cartilage; the other kidney compensates.
Acquired cystic disease develops in end-stage kidneys on long-term dialysis and raises the risk of renal cell carcinoma.
Bilateral renal agenesis removes fetal urine, causing oligohydramnios and Potter sequence; pulmonary hypoplasia causes death.
A single kidney grows by hypertrophy and hyperfiltration of existing nephrons, because no new nephrons form after about 36 weeks of gestation.

Primary VUR results from a short intravesical ureter that defeats the flap valve, causing recurrent pyelonephritis and polar reflux nephropathy scars; the voiding cystourethrogram diagnoses and grades it.

verify: Proportions of Alport inheritance (X-linked about 80%, autosomal recessive about 15%, autosomal dominant the remainder) vary among sources; recent genetic studies suggest autosomal dominant COL4A3 and COL4A4 disease is more common than older texts state.
Age at end-stage renal disease in X-linked males is given as about 20 to 40 years in this chapter; sources range from the second to the fifth decade depending on mutation type.
The rate of anti-GBM disease after transplantation in Alport syndrome is quoted as a few percent; values vary.
ADPKD prevalence (about 1 in 400 to 1 in 1,000), the PKD1 share (about 78 to 85%), and the delay in PKD2 disease (about 15 to 20 years) vary among sources.

Prevalence of intracranial aneurysm in ADPKD is given as about 10% here; Robbins gives a wider range (about 10% to 30%), and family history raises the risk. Mitral valve prolapse prevalence (about 20 to 25%) is not stated as a number in the chapter.
The two-hit model of cyst formation is the most widely taught explanation; dosage and threshold models of polycystin function are also proposed.
Incidence figures for ARPKD (about 1 in 20,000), unilateral renal agenesis (about 1 in 1,000), and VUR (about 1% of children, about one third of children with febrile UTI) are approximate.
Timing of fetal urine as the main source of amniotic fluid (about 16 weeks) and end of nephrogenesis (about 34 to 36 weeks) vary slightly among embryology texts.
The VUR grading table follows the International Reflux Study classification; confirm whether NABNE expects grade definitions or only the concept of grading.

The magnitude of renal cell carcinoma risk in acquired cystic disease is stated only as markedly higher; Robbins gives about 7% of patients over 10 years of dialysis, and relative risk estimates vary widely.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: ureterovesical-junction (normal oblique tunnel versus short tunnel with reflux) and cystic-kidneys (ADPKD, ARPKD, and multicystic dysplastic kidney side by side).
